title: What is known about 1RB1LD_0RC0LF_1LD1RE_0LA0RB_0RD1RB_0LD---
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB1LD_0RC0LF_1LD1RE_0LA0RB_0RD1RB_0LD---.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state machine halts from blank tape. This page records what is established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.

The machine is a pair of counters. The head lives near the start cell and makes round trips: one to the left, where it adds one to a binary counter written in 4-cell digits, and one to the right, where it updates a second, more complicated representation of a counter. The left counter is understood exactly (its three moves are proved in Lean and checked over 8 million visits); the right one is not.
verdict: The question is open. The machine is a rewriting system on the right half of its tape (the visit law, proved in Lean): it halts only if a visit meets 111. Its first four rules are those of the three machines that busycoq PR59 proves to halt in round 161,211 on the block 1011; this machine rewrites 1011 to 1000 instead and, in an accelerated run (computed, not proved), carries on: no halt up to round 200,000. No halt in the first 1010 steps of a direct run.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (F1); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: The three moves of the left counter
claims.text: For every n and any tape around them: increment L 1000 (1010)^n 1 D>0 R reaches L 1010 1 (0001)^n E>0 R (n trailing one-digits become zero-digits, the zero-digit before them becomes a one); overflow without prefix 0^inf (1010)^n 1 D>0 R reaches 0^inf 1 0 1 (0001)^n 0 D> R; overflow with the prefix 10 0^inf 1 0 (1010)^n 1 D>0 R reaches 0^inf 1 0 1 0 0 (0100)^n 0 C> R. Each is a theorem about the machine's step function with an exact step count.

claims.title: The machine as a carry system: eight local rules
claims.text: Write > for the head in state B about to read the next cell, and < for the head in state D on the cell before the mark. Between two such moments the machine does exactly one of: R1 >011 → 011>; R2 >0100 → 011>0; R3 >0101 → 0100>; R4 >00 → 0<1; R5 0>1 → <00; L1 10< → <10; L2 00< → 1>0; L3 1< → 0>. Each is a Lean theorem about the machine's step function, with its number of steps (3, 5, 4, 2, 2, 2, 2, 1), for every tape around the cells shown. The cases cover everything B or D can read, except B on a 1 that has a 1 on its left (the halt, next claim).

claims.title: The halting pattern
claims.text: From B about to read 0 1 1 1 the machine halts four steps later, whatever else is on the tape. Reading the table backwards (an argument on paper, not in Lean), every halt comes about this way: F is entered only from B on a 1, and a B that reads a 1 with a 1 on its left was entered from E on a 1, E from C on a 1, C from B on a 0. In the carry system: the halt is rule R1 applied in front of a 1.

claims.title: Blocks of 3-cell digits count in binary
claims.text: For every k and any tape around: after a 1, the block (010)^(k+1) 00 hit by B becomes (000)^(k+1) 01, with D back on its first cell, in 10k + 12 steps. Read 010 as the digit one and 000 as zero, lowest digit first: k+1 ones followed by a zero become k+1 zeros followed by a one. This is the carry of the right half; the left half's carry (4-cell digits) is the claim on the three moves of the left counter.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: The visit law: the machine as a rewriting system
claims.text: A visit (the head enters a stream s in state C with a 0 on its left and returns in state A two cells further left) rewrites the stream by 0 s → 1 s, 100 s → 000 v(s), 110 s → 000 v(s), 1010 s → 1010 v(v(s)), 1011 s → 1000 s, for every stream and every tape to the left. 111 s halts the machine. The six prefixes 0, 100, 110, 111, 1010 and 1011 cover every stream, so these rules are the whole machine: it can halt only when a visit meets 111. From blank tape the run is a sequence of rounds 0∞ A> 1 0 S → 0∞ A> 1 0 v(1 0 S), starting from S = 1 0∞ after 4 steps.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>10</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/tmrun.c runs 1010 steps from blank tape without a halt; at the end the tape holds only 91 ones.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 252 cells have been visited and 77 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: Where a halt can be
claims.text: A closed tape language of windows of 5 cells (tools/py/bbtools/ctl.py, closure checked by the script, not by Lean) contains every configuration reachable from blank tape, and its only halting configurations have F reading a 1 with a 0 and then a 1 left of the head and a 1 right of it (0 1 F>1 1).

claims.title: The left half is a binary counter of round trips
claims.text: Every time D reads the 0 at cell 1 with a 1 at cell 0 (the head about to visit the left half), the cells from the left end to cell 0 read (10)? w 1 with w a word of 4-cell digits 1010 (one) and 1000 (zero), least significant digit next to the centre. In the first 109 steps this happens 8,388,630 times and every time the number w is one more than the time before, except 45 growth moves, all of the two kinds above: 10+all ones (b digits) becomes all ones with b+1 digits and no prefix, which overflows at the next visit to 10 + b+1 zeros.

claims.title: The left end grows at 2<sup>k</sup> and 3·2<sup>k−1</sup> round trips
claims.text: Counting the visits above as round trips T = 1, 2, 3, ..., the left end of the tape grows (by two cells) exactly when T is 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 16, 24, ..., 2<sup>k</sup>, 3·2<sup>k−1</sup>, ... up to T = 12,582,912 (all 46 growths in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps). A round trip costs 135 to 225 steps on average, so the left end grows like the logarithm of the step count.

claims.title: Not decided by n-gram CPS up to width 14
claims.text: The n-gram Closed Position Set decider (tools/c/ngramcps.c) with equal widths 4, 6, 8, 10, 12 and 14, plain and with the fixed-length (1) and LRU history augmentations, either reaches a halting local configuration (UNKNOWN) or stops at 3·107 local configurations: it does not prove non-halting at these settings.

claims.title: The eight rules replay the run
claims.text: A program that knows only the eight rules applies them 3·107 times from the start 1>; the steps they stand for add up to 73,332,821, and at every millionth application the tape, head and state equal those of the plain machine after the same number of steps. Rules used: L1 10,000,057; L2 3,333,457; L3 3,333,200; R1 218; R2 3,332,982; R3 3,333,428; R4 3,333,458; R5 3,333,200.

claims.title: R1, the only way to a halt, is rare
claims.text: R1 is the entry E1 of the table (E reading a 1). In the first 1010 steps it is used 424 times (5 times in the first 103 steps, 18 in 104, 46 in 105, 90 in 106, 148 in 107, 228 in 108, 306 in 109), first at step 77, and each time the cell after the 011 is a 0 (the run does not halt). So a halt can only happen at these rare moments.

claims.title: It does not halt where the PR59 machines halt
claims.text: The first four rules are also the rules of the three machines that busycoq PR59 proves to halt (they halt on 1011, in round 161,211). An accelerated simulator of the visit law (counts of visits kept as 2e − c; rules learned from the table; checked against a direct run, against exact integers for 1,500 rounds, and against PR59's halting round on the reference machine) finds: rounds 1 to 161,210 use only the four shared rules, round 161,211 meets 1011 at the right end of the word, writes 1000 and continues. Observed: no halt and no visit to 111 up to round 200,000. Computed, not proved.

claims.title: Growth shape: exp/exp
claims.text: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the logarithm of the step count: each new cell costs a roughly constant factor more time, the signature of a counter or of a Collatz-like map whose values are written on the tape (fitted exponent 0.075). Right of the start it grows like the logarithm of the step count: each new cell costs a roughly constant factor more time, the signature of a counter or of a Collatz-like map whose values are written on the tape (fitted exponent 0.065).

claims.title: A gap growing by 3
claims.text: At the left records at 9.9·107, 1.4·108, 2.0·108 and 2.7·108 steps the longest gap shortly after the (1 0)^n stretch has 19, 22, 25 and 28 zeros. This gap is the lowest right-hand segment emptied out (all digits 000) just after an overflow, and it gains one 3-cell digit per growth.

claims.title: The right half: a chain of counter segments
claims.text: Right of the centre the tape is a chain of segments, each a binary counter with 3-cell digits (one of 100, 010, 001 for a one, depending on the segment, and 000 for a zero), least significant digit nearest the centre, separated by short markers such as 101 and 010 100. The lowest segment changes on every round trip; a segment that overflows carries into the next one. At each growth of the left end the lowest segments are re-laid (one segment gains a digit and changes its phase). The right end grows at irregular values of T (974, 1277, 1405, 1903, ..., 8,360,447, 14,168,192), not at powers of 2. The rule for the re-laying has not been found.
claims.where: c/rightgrow.c; read off snapshots, not checked mechanically

claims.title: Does it halt from blank tape?
claims.text: Not known. In the carry system the question reads: does B ever come to stand in front of 0 1 1 1, that is, is rule R1 ever applied in front of a 1? Answering it needs a description of the right half as numbers (which digits sit where when R1 fires), and that has not been found. The community tracker says this machine equals Beaver Math Olympiad problem 10, 'a seven-rule carry system' with rules proved in Rocq; we have not seen that statement, so we cannot say how its seven rules group our eight, nor what arithmetic form it gives the question.

claims.title: Related holdouts
claims.text: The same tapes at another pace, whatever the states, as 5 other holdouts (listed on the explainer page).

check: gcc -O2 -o vis holdouts/1RB0LB_0RC0LD_1LD1RE_0LA0RF_1RB0RD_0RB---/c/vis.c && (ulimit -s unlimited; ./vis 1RB1LD_0RC0LF_1LD1RE_0LA0RB_0RD1RB_0LD--- 200000)   # accelerated run to round 200,000, about 45 minutes

explainer.lede: Nobody knows. This machine is a small rewriting system: blocks 000/100 that act as binary digits and blocks 1010 that double the visits passing through. Three sister machines with the same four rules are proved to halt in round 161,211 on the block 1011; this one rewrites that block and runs on.

facts.text: The visit law: the machine as a rewriting system on streams.
No halt in the accelerated run; the PR59 machines halt in round 161,211.
No halt in the C simulator.
No halt, proved in Lean; the first 10,000 by the kernel alone.

sections.eyebrow: The whole machine in a few rules
sections.heading: The visit law
html: Forget the states for a moment. Call everything from some cell to the right a stream. Whenever the head steps into a stream in state C with a 0 behind it, it comes back out in state A two cells further left, and the only thing that has changed is the stream. That excursion is a visit, and what it does depends only on how the stream begins (proved in Lean for every stream):

the stream beginsafter the visitLean
0 s1 svis_0
100 s000 then one visit to svis_100
110 s000 then one visit to svis_110
1010 s1010 then two visits to svis_1010
1011 s1000 svis_1011
111 sthe machine haltsvis_111_halts

So a block 000/100 is a binary digit: it passes every second visit on. A block 1010 is a doubler: it passes every visit on twice. 111 s halts the machine. The six prefixes 0, 100, 110, 111, 1010 and 1011 cover every stream, so these rules are the whole machine: it can halt only when a visit meets 111.

The run from blank tape is a sequence of rounds: the tape is 0∞ A> 1 0 S, and one round puts 1 0 in front of S and makes one visit. After k rounds S begins with k copies of 10, that is k/2 doublers, so 2k/2 visits reach the word behind them. That word is the right-hand counter of the earlier descriptions.

The same rules, a different ending. The three machines that busycoq PR59 proves to halt have the same first four rules; they halt when a visit meets 1011, which first happens in round 161,211. This machine writes 1000 there instead. In our accelerated run (computed, checked three ways, not proved) it does exactly that in round 161,211 and carries on; no halt up to round 200,000.

sections.heading: Two counters and a messenger
html: Watch the simulator for a few thousand steps and you will see the head shuttle around the start cell. Each shuttle (a round trip) goes once to the left and once to the right. On the left it adds 1 to a number written in binary; on the right it adds 1 to a second record of the same count, written in a different and messier way. Both ends of the tape grow only when a counter needs a new digit, so the tape grows like the logarithm of the time: after 1010 steps it holds only 91 ones.

sections.heading: The machine as a carry system
html: Two moments recur in the run: the head in state B moving right, written > in front of the cell it is about to read, and the head in state D moving left, written < after the cell it is on. From one such moment to the next the machine takes between one and five steps and does one of eight things:

rulebeforeafterin words
R1>011011>pass over 011
R2>0100011>0a digit one becomes 011 and the hit moves on: a carry
R3>01010100>erase the 1 after 010 and go on
R4>000<1turn round on 00, leaving 01
R50>1<00erase a 1 and go back two cells
L110<<10skip a pair 10
L200<1>0turn round on 00, leaving 10
L31<0>erase a 1 and turn round
halt>0111R1 in front of a 1
Each rule is proved in Lean for every tape around the cells shown, and a program that knows only these rules reproduces 73 million steps of the machine exactly. The start from blank tape is 1>.

Counting with these rules. Take three cells 000 as the digit zero and 010 as the digit one, lowest digit on the left, with a 1 standing before the block. A hit on 000 turns round at once and leaves 010 (R4, then L1). A hit on 010 turns it into 011 and passes the hit to the next digit (R2); when the hit finally turns round, the way back erases every 011 to 000 (L1, L3, R5 in turn). So 010 010 010 000 becomes 000 000 000 010: seven plus one is eight. Lean proves this for any number of ones (carry). The left half counts the same way with pairs: L1 skips pairs 10, L2 turns the first 00 it meets into 10, and R3 on the way back turns every second pair into 00, which is the binary counter of round trips in 4-cell digits (1010 one, 1000 zero).

Where it could stop. The machine halts exactly when B stands in front of 0111: it passes 011 by R1 and finds a 1 where a 0 or a fresh digit should start. R1 itself is rare: 424 uses in the first 1010 steps, against hundreds of millions of uses of every other rule, and each time the next cell was a 0. In a plain block of digits R1 never fires, because 011 exists only while a carry is on its way; in the round trips we traced by hand it fires where blocks of different alignment meet. Which meetings are possible is the part that is not understood.

The neighbours. busycoq holds proofs for three machines that differ from this one in a single entry: E1 = 0RF (SOMDCv1.v, a closed family of configurations with period 7) and E1 = 1RF (RRBAv3.v), both non-halting, and F0 = 1RD (Eqv_v2.v, shown equivalent to a solved machine). E1 is exactly rule R1, used from step 77 on, and F0 is half of rule R5, used in a ninth of all rule applications, so none of those proofs applies to this machine's run: their machines behave differently from the first hundred steps.

sections.heading: Binary in blocks of four cells
html: Left of the start the tape reads, from the far end, an optional 10 and then digits of four cells: 1010 means 1 and 1000 means 0, followed by a single 1 next to the centre. The digit next to the centre is the least significant. For example, at step 87,153 the left half reads 10 1010 1010 1010 1000 1010 1010 1000 1000 1000 1: the binary number 111011000 (472). At the next visit, step 87,179, the last digit has become 1010: 111011001 (473).

To add one, the head comes in from the centre in state D, walks left in state A over the trailing ones, turns the first 1000 into 1010, and walks back in state E turning each 1010 it passed into 1000. That is ordinary binary carrying, and Lean proves it for any number n of trailing ones (left_increment).

visitleft half (digits)value
T10 1000 1010 1010 1011 = 3
T+110 1010 1000 1000 1100 = 4

When all digits are ones the counter overflows and the tape grows by two cells at the left end. Because a digit is four cells, this happens in two half-steps: with the prefix 10 the ones become one more digit of ones (no prefix), and at the next visit those overflow to 10 followed by zeros. So the left end grows exactly when the number of round trips is 2k or 3·2k−1: 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 16, 24, ... This was checked for all 8,388,630 visits in the first 109 steps.

sections.heading: The same count, kept in segments
html: Right of the start the tape is a chain of segments. Each segment is again a binary counter, now with 3-cell digits: a one is 100, 010 or 001 (the segment decides which; the three are the same pattern shifted by a cell) and a zero is 000. Segments are separated by short markers like 101. The lowest segment changes every round trip, and when it overflows the carry runs into the next segment, which is why the head occasionally makes a much longer trip to the right.

What makes the machine hard is what happens at the growth moments of the left counter: then the lowest right segments are rewritten, one of them gains a digit and changes from one shifted pattern to another. This re-laying makes the right end grow at irregular times (round trips 974, 1277, 1405, 1903, ..., 14,168,192) instead of at powers of two. No rule for it has been found yet.

sections.heading: Where it could stop
html: The machine stops only if F reads a 1. F never occurs in the moves of the left counter, so a halt would have to happen right of the left counter, in a pattern 0 1 F>1 1 (the closed tape language of 5-cell windows rules out every other place). Two neighbouring 1s are rare on this tape. Proving that it never halts would need the full rule of the right segments: what a carry does at each kind of marker and how the segments are re-laid when the left counter grows. If that rule is as regular as the left counter, the machine runs forever; nothing found so far says otherwise, but it is not known.

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the logarithm of the step count: each new cell costs a roughly constant factor more time, the signature of a counter or of a Collatz-like map whose values are written on the tape (fitted exponent 0.075). Right of the start it grows like the logarithm of the step count: each new cell costs a roughly constant factor more time, the signature of a counter or of a Collatz-like map whose values are written on the tape (fitted exponent 0.065).
After 109 steps the tape spans 252 cells (90 left of the start, 156 right), with a density of 1s of 0.306.
These are measurements of one bounded run, sorted by tools/py/bbtools/triage.py; the macro structure behind them is the next thing to find.

sections.heading: Related machines
html: Other holdouts of the list of 608 that are tied to this one. The comparison of tables is exact; everything about runs was checked on the first 107 steps of each machine and is an observation, not a proof (holdouts/related.py, holdouts/related.json).

Same tapes at another pace (observed, not proved). Leave the states aside and compare only the tape and the place of the head. Then a large part of the first 107 configurations of this machine are configurations of the machines below, in the same order and up to the end of the run. The steps at which they occur differ, the tables are not renamings of each other, and equal tapes with different states may be continued differently, so this does not tie the halting questions together.

summary: A rewriting system on streams (visit law, proved in Lean): the first four rules are those of the PR59 machines that halt on 1011 in round 161,211; this one rewrites 1011 to 1000 and runs on (computed: no halt up to round 200,000); it halts only if a visit meets 111; open.
